svg.text: Reading a blood gas in three steps
Lungs move carbon dioxide in minutes. Kidneys move bicarbonate over days.
Step 1 — look at the pH
Below 7.35 the patient is acidotic. Above 7.45 alkalotic. Normal 7.35 to 7.45.
The pH tells you which way. It does not tell you which organ.
Step 2 — who caused it?
Look at the carbon dioxide, normal 4.7 to 6.0 kPa
Look at the bicarbonate, normal 22 to 26 mmol/L
Whichever one has moved the SAME way as
the pH is the culprit
Low pH with high CO2 = respiratory acidosis
Step 3 — is the other one compensating?
If the other value has moved the OPPOSITE way,
the body is trying to correct the problem
pH still abnormal = partial compensation
pH back to normal = full compensation
Compensation never overshoots. It corrects
The four pictures, and the Ghanaian ward where you meet them
Metabolic acidosis
low pH, low bicarbonate — cholera, severe diarrhoea, DKA, sepsis, kidney failure
Metabolic alkalosis
high pH, high bicarbonate — prolonged vomiting, pyloric obstruction, water tablets
Respiratory acidosis
low pH, high CO2 — the patient is not ventilating: opioids, severe asthma, exhaustion
Respiratory alkalosis
high pH, low CO2 — over-breathing: pain, anxiety, early sepsis, salicylate
Deep sighing breathing in a dehydrated child is the lungs blowing off acid. Treat the cause, not the breathing.
